object_types.name: Account
object_types.definition: A customer account in the billing system, identified by an account number. Every account can have multiple subscriptions (one per product).

source_references.excerpt: An account. Every account has an account number. That's what everything hangs off... Yes. Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: AccountNumber
object_types.definition: The unique numeric identifier for an account, six digits, sequential, never reused.

source_references.excerpt: Every account has an account number... Six digits, sequential, never reused.

object_types.name: Subscription
object_types.definition: An agreement that an account pays a specified amount on a billing cycle for a product. Identified by subscription ID.

source_references.excerpt: A subscription is the agreement that this account pays us this amount on this cycle for this thing. It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: SubscriptionId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a subscription, generated with prefix SUB.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a subscription ID... Unique. Generated, prefixed with SUB.

object_types.name: Product
object_types.definition: A product offering, identified by product code. Currently three products: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT... Fixed today.

object_types.name: ProductCode
object_types.definition: The code identifying a product, one of: CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT... Fixed today.

object_types.name: PricePlan
object_types.definition: The billing artifact specifying what a customer pays and how often, identified by plan code. For example, CORE-MO-49 (monthly) or CORE-AN-490 (annual). Each price plan points to exactly one feature bundle.

source_references.excerpt: The price plan. It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: PlanCode
object_types.definition: The unique code identifying a price plan, such as CORE-MO-49 or CORE-AN-490.

source_references.excerpt: It's got a plan code, it says what the customer pays and how often. CORE-MO-49, CORE-AN-490, that kind of thing.

object_types.name: FeatureBundle
object_types.definition: A feature tier that defines what a customer gets: number of seats, API access, SSO, etc. The product-facing tier on the pricing page. Identified by name.

source_references.excerpt: When I say plan I mean what the customer gets. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. It's the feature bundle -- how many seats, whether they get the API, whether they get SSO.

object_types.name: BundleName
object_types.definition: The name of a feature bundle: Starter, Professional, or Enterprise.

source_references.excerpt: Name. Starter, Professional, Enterprise. There's no code, which annoys me... Yes. There's exactly one Professional.

object_types.name: PlanChange
object_types.definition: A record of a change to a subscription's plan, capturing the new price plan, effective date, and who requested it. Identified by change ID.

source_references.excerpt: So a plan change is its own thing, with its own identity?... It's got a change ID... It records the subscription, the new price plan, the effective date, and who requested it.

object_types.name: ChangeId
object_types.definition: The unique identifier for a plan change record.

source_references.excerpt: So a plan change is its own thing, with its own identity?... It's got a change ID. It has to, because we need to know who made it and when it takes effect

object_types.name: SubscriptionStatus
object_types.definition: The current state of a subscription. Exactly one of: trialing, active, past due, cancelled.

source_references.excerpt: Trialing, active, past due, cancelled... Exactly one, yes.

object_types.name: BillingPeriod
object_types.definition: The frequency of billing for a subscription. Exactly one of: monthly, annual.

source_references.excerpt: Monthly or annual... Only those two... Every subscription has exactly one billing period.

object_types.name: StartDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription becomes effective. Always required; cannot be null.

source_references.excerpt: Start date... Start date is always there. You can't create a subscription without one, the form won't submit.

object_types.name: EndDate
object_types.definition: The date a subscription ends or is cancelled. Optional; null for open-ended subscriptions.

source_references.excerpt: End date, sometimes... An open-ended subscription has no end date. Most of them are open-ended -- they run until cancelled.

object_types.name: EffectiveDate
object_types.definition: The date on which a plan change takes effect. May differ from the date the change was requested.

source_references.excerpt: We write a plan change with an effective date... Someone can make a change on the third that takes effect on the first of next month.

object_types.name: Requester
object_types.definition: The person or system that requested a plan change.

ambiguities.description: Composite uniqueness for active subscriptions. The constraint 'one active subscription per account per product' involves three concepts: Account, Product, and Subscription status. It is unclear whether this is best modeled as: (1) a composite external uniqueness spanning Account, Product, and the 'active' status value; (2) a ternary fact type grouping these three dimensions; or (3) separate binary fact types with a rule layered on top. The database enforces it at the application level, but the conceptual structure is ambiguous.

source_references.excerpt: An account can have a subscription to each of them at once... One active subscription per account per product, enforced at the database level.

ambiguities.name: Plan ambiguity - three meanings
ambiguities.description: The term 'plan' is used with three distinct meanings: (1) Price Plan (what the customer pays and billing frequency, e.g., CORE-MO-49); (2) Feature Bundle (what the customer gets, e.g., Professional tier with features like seats, API, SSO); (3) Sales deal plan (what the sales team negotiated, which frequently matches neither). The model captures (1) and (2) with different names, but the term 'plan' in stakeholder speech remains overloaded. This may cause future confusion during requirements elicitation and documentation.

source_references.excerpt: Priya, what's a plan?... The price plan... When I say plan I mean what the customer gets... We've got two things both called plan, and the sales team calls a third thing a plan, which is the deal they negotiated, which frequently matches neither.

ambiguities.description: Paused subscription state. Priya states that 'paused' is a separate boolean flag, not a status value, yet it behaves like one and is conflated with the active status (paused subscriptions appear in 'active' queries). It is unclear whether paused is an orthogonal property that can coexist with any status, or whether it should be modeled as a fifth status. The transcript notes that this ambiguity causes bugs.

source_references.excerpt: There's also paused... Paused isn't a status, it's a flag... It behaves like a status... it's a separate boolean, which is exactly why it causes bugs. If you ask the system for active subscriptions you get paused ones too.

ambiguities.description: Refund policy for mid-term annual subscription cancellations. The system rule is clear: cancellation sets an end date and access runs to the paid-through date with no automatic refund. However, the business rule is undecided. Finance requires refund policy to be defined (for contra-revenue vs. refund liability accounting), but legal and finance must decide whether the rule is: run-to-term (current), prorated refund, or credit. Four refunds were granted as goodwill in the prior quarter, suggesting an emerging undocumented policy. This must be resolved before the model can capture the true business rule.

source_references.excerpt: Someone signs an annual deal in January, pays up front, cancels in April. What happens?... Nothing happens... It becomes one when the customer escalates and we give them a refund anyway, which we did four times last quarter... the system rule is clear, and what's unclear is whether the system rule is the business rule.

ambiguities.description: Current plan maintenance on subscription. Sam initially questioned whether a subscription has a current price plan, noting that changes are the history. Priya clarified that a denormalised current plan field exists and is maintained by the change process. However, the relationship between the current plan field and the change history creates a potential consistency issue: if they ever disagree, the change history is the source of truth and the current plan is the bug. This raises the question: should current plan be stored, or derived on-the-fly from change history? The model follows the statement that it is stored and maintained, but this is a temporal modeling concern that may need periodic reconciliation.

source_references.excerpt: You said a subscription belongs to one price plan. It doesn't, really -- that's what the plan changes are for... No, Sam, it does have a current plan field. The changes are the history, but there's a denormalised current plan on the record... And if those two ever disagree, the change history wins and the current plan is the bug.

ambiguities.description: Feature bundle existence vs. pricing. A feature bundle can exist without any price plan pointing to it (Enterprise existed for two months before pricing). Conversely, price plans always entitle exactly one bundle. This creates an asymmetric relationship: bundles are optional partners, price plans are mandatory. The model captures this, but it may be worth clarifying whether unpriced bundles are a normal part of the product lifecycle (build first, price later) or an edge case.

source_references.excerpt: Can a bundle exist with no price plan pointing at it?... Yes -- we build a bundle before we price it. Enterprise existed for two months before there was anything to buy.

ambiguities.description: Product code fixed set. Tom states the current product catalog is fixed at three products (CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT), but a fourth is in discovery. The model captures the value constraint as [CORE, ANALYTICS, CONNECT], but this constraint will need to be updated when the fourth product launches. Is the constraint on the Product entity type itself, or on a specific time window? The model treats it as a universal constraint, which may need to become time-dependent or versioned.

source_references.excerpt: Product code. We have three: CORE, ANALYTICS, and CONNECT... Fixed today. There's a fourth in discovery, but I'm not going to pretend I know what it is.

ambiguities.description: Account number reuse. Priya states account numbers are never reused: if an account closes and the company returns, they get a new number. This is a business rule enforced for revenue recognition. However, it is unclear whether there is any historical linkage between the old and new accounts (for auditing or customer relationship tracking), or whether they are treated as completely independent entities. The model treats them as separate, but reconciliation logic may exist upstream.

source_references.excerpt: Six digits, sequential, never reused. If an account closes and the same company comes back, they get a new number and we treat them as a new customer for reporting... It drives finance the other way. If we reused numbers, revenue recognition would be a nightmare.
